A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same transformer realization of clustering algorithms despite the title change. Their text, figures, tables, equations, and complete appendices support reliable comparison.

before.justification: Section 2.3 and Figures 3–4 report original numerical validation against Lloyd’s algorithm and experiments varying temperature, dimensionality, sample count, cluster count, and scaling.

after.justification: V2 retains numerical validation and adds original training, ablation, distribution-transfer, and OpenML experiments in Section 2.3 and Appendices B and I.

M1.justification: V1 prescribes transformer weights and leaves learning for future work. V2 adds learning of Q/K/V matrices using a smoothed k-means loss and iterative reuse of a trained single-layer model, resetting auxiliary embeddings between clustering steps (Appendix B). The handcrafted constructions largely remain. Section 2.4 specifies a rectified-quadratic FFN, inconsistently with Appendix F’s retained ordinary-quadratic construction.

E1.justification: Beyond v1’s synthetic numerical validation, v2 evaluates transfer to Cauchy, Laplace, Gumbel, and lognormal mixtures and 15 OpenML datasets (Appendix B.4). Appendix I additionally evaluates robust clustering and randomized k-medoids on 10 OpenML datasets; these algorithms were only developed theoretically in v1.

E2.justification: Lloyd’s remains the main comparator. V2 Table 4 adds an evaluated comparison between robust k-means and trimmed k-means, which v1 presented without experimental comparison. The k-means++ experiment changes initialization of the retained methods. PAM and CLARANS remain cited methods rather than evaluated baselines.

E3.justification: New learning experiments introduce 10,000 training steps, batches of 32 clustering tasks, 320 validation tasks, and synthetic evaluation over 20 clustering steps. V2 also tests k-means++ initialization and specifies OpenML subsampling to at most 1024 points and 32 features with 10 clustering steps. These are added protocols, not demonstrated changes to v1’s retained validation.

E4.justification: V1’s parameter-sensitivity analysis survives as v2 Figure 7. V2 adds embedding-dimension ablations, loss-temperature and training-convergence studies, distribution-transfer tests, learned-weight and attention-map analyses, and sensitivity to robust-clustering parameters and the medoid sampling gap (Figures 4–6, 8–10; Tables 4–5).

E5.justification: V1 explains error bars through variation across parameter settings. V2 adds training curves aggregated over 10 random trials with interquartile ribbons, min–max ranges over 320 test tasks, and mean±standard deviation over 40 OpenML trials. Tables 4–5 additionally disclose aggregation over 10 trials.

E6.justification: V2 adds substantial results for the learned model and existing algorithm variants. Table 1 reports average log objectives of 5.0052 versus Lloyd’s 5.2636 on Gaussian tasks, but 3.3443 versus 3.2528 on Cauchy tasks. Table 2 favors Lloyd’s on all 15 OpenML datasets. Tables 4–5 add robust-clustering and medoid results. These are new comparisons, not same-setting improvements over v1.

T1.justification: The central equivalence proofs are substantially retained, including v1’s dot-product construction in v2 Appendix F. Limited additions include the O(d+k) size corollary, the smoothed training objective and its limiting relation, and dot-product parameter invariance in Remark E.1. V2 also removes v1’s preliminary pairwise-similarity-to-k-means derivation.

C1.justification: V1 claims exact handcrafted implementations and architectural routes to clustering variants, explicitly deferring learnability. V2’s abstract, contributions, and conclusion additionally claim that training produces a generalizable clustering algorithm outperforming Lloyd’s on new tasks. Compact model size is also foregrounded, expanding the contribution from constructive expressivity to learned clustering effectiveness.

C2.justification: V2 interprets learned attention sparsity and weight structure, explains sensitivity through loss smoothing, and attributes OpenML underperformance to training-distribution mismatch. Its limitations explicitly distinguish empirical learning from unproved generalization guarantees and state that transfer to larger cluster counts is unsupported. These replace v1’s broader deferral of learnability with substantive mechanisms and applicability boundaries.

D1.justification: V2 adds a code repository link and a detailed training recipe: mixture-generation steps, normalization to the unit hypercube, loss temperatures, learning-rate decay, training budgets, and iterative inference instructions. OpenML sampling procedures are also documented. V1 provides prescribed weights and mentions PyTorch but lacks these training and access details.

R1.justification: V2 substantially reframes positioning around compact constructive expressivity relative to universal approximation and Turing-completeness results. It adds that literature, further in-context-learning references, and clustering-initialization references, while removing v1’s extended mechanistic-interpretability framing and RASP/ALTA comparison. The change exceeds bibliographic updates to retained works.

P1.justification: V2 retitles the paper and substantially rewrites the abstract, introduction, and discussion, adding explicit contributions and a separate conclusion. Box 1 becomes explanatory prose, the existing dot-product construction gains a main-text section, and the single Methods appendix is reorganized into thematic appendices with a contents page.

P2.justification: V2 adds learning and diagnostic Figures 4–6 and 8–10 and results Tables 1, 2, 4, and 5. V1 Figures 4–5 and Table 1 are relocated as v2 Figures 7 and 11 and Table 3, with an appendix-reference column added to the table. Figure 3 is redrawn, captions expand, and boxed presentation changes substantially.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially addresses the learnability question explicitly left open in v1. Controlled learning comparisons, embedding ablations, and repeated-trial reporting establish practical capabilities, while Cauchy and OpenML failures clarify their boundaries. Added implementation details and the code link improve reproducibility. The unreconciled rectified-versus-ordinary quadratic FFN description is a weakness, but the gains in empirical support and understanding are substantial.
